raw_segments.text: He was the only man of us who still followed the sea.
The worst that could be said of him was that he did not represent his class.
He was a seaman, but he was a wanderer, too, while most seamen lead, if one may so express
it, a sedentary life.
Their minds are of the stay-at-home order, and their home is always with them—the ship.
And so is their country—the sea.
One ship is very much like another, and the sea is always the same.
In the immutability of their surroundings the foreign shores, the foreign faces, the
changing immensity of life, glide past, veiled not by a sense of mystery but by a slightly
disdainful ignorance.
For there is nothing mysterious to a seaman unless it be the sea itself, which is the
mistress of his existence and as inscrutable as destiny.
For the rest, after his hours of work, a casual stroll or a casual spree on shore suffices
to unfold for him the secret of a whole continent, and generally he finds the secret not worth
knowing.
The yarns of seamen have a direct simplicity, the whole meaning of which lies within the
shell of a cracked nut.
But Marlowe was not typical, if his propensity to spin yarns be accepted.
And to him, the meaning of an episode was not inside like a kernel, but outside, enveloping
the tail which brought it out only as a glow brings out a haze, in the likeness of one
of these misty halos that sometimes are made visible by the spectral illumination of moonshine.
